title: The Quart Pot to the Abbey Nave: Woolsthorpe, the Plague Years, and the Master of the Mint
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Woolsthorpe Manor, the birth in the quart pot
stops.date_confidence: attested; 25 December 1642 Old Style, the Julian calendar England kept until 1752, which is 4 January 1643 New Style. Sources disagree over which to lead with and the disagreement is not an error in any of them.
stops.campa: In a small stone farmhouse near Colsterworth, three months after his father is buried, a son is born to Hannah Ayscough and named for the dead man. He arrives early and so small that nobody expects him to keep breathing through the night; his mother says afterwards that he could have been fitted into a quart pot. Two women sent to Lady Pakenham's for medicine sit down on the way, certain there will be no child alive to give it to. The manor is a yeoman's holding of sheep and barley. No one in the house can read a Latin sentence.
sources: MacTutor (University of St Andrews), biography of Newton
Richard S. Westfall, Never at Rest (1980), cited through the research pool
National Trust, Woolsthorpe Manor site history
suggested_refs: Woolsthorpe Manor, Woolsthorpe-by-Colsterworth, Lincolnshire, the birth room preserved by the National Trust

stops.name: Colsterworth, the baptism of a dead man's son
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Colsterworth parish register, 1 January 1643 Old Style, one week after the birth
stops.campa: At the parish church of St John the Baptist the infant is carried to the font and entered in the register as the son of the late Isaac Newton, yeoman. The clerk uses the ordinary formula for a posthumous child, so the register carries the father's death and the son's name in the same line. Into the same church, sixteen years later, he cuts a sundial plate that the parish still keeps, scoring the hours into the stone with a knife while the sermon runs on above him.
sources: Colsterworth parish register, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: The Newton sundial plate in St John the Baptist, Colsterworth, cut by the boy at about nine

stops.name: North Witham, the mother goes to the rector
stops.date_confidence: attested, 27 January 1646, in the parish of North Witham. The chronology lens of the research pool gave 1645; the parish record and MacTutor's 'age two' both support 1646.
stops.campa: Hannah Ayscough marries Barnabas Smith, the elderly rector of North Witham, and moves two and a half miles south to his parsonage. The boy is three years and one month old and does not go with her. He is left at Woolsthorpe with his grandmother, and stays there eight years while his mother raises a second family in another man's house. What he thinks of it survives in his own hand, sixteen years later, in a list of sins he sets down before taking communion, where the rectory at North Witham appears between a mousetrap and a pie.
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: The rectory of North Witham, Barnabas Smith's parsonage, where Hannah lived until 1653

stops.name: Grantham, the apothecary's lodger
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. MacTutor places a return to the Grantham school nearer 1653, the year Barnabas Smith died; no reachable source reconciles the two dates.
stops.campa: He boards with the apothecary Clark on the High Street and walks to the King's School to learn Latin, Greek, and a little arithmetic. He is not first in the class at the start. He is first in the town at making things: model windmills driven by a mouse on a treadwheel, water clocks, paper lanterns flown at night to frighten the country people, sundials cut on every wall he can reach. He carves his name into a windowsill that the school still shows. The walls of his lodging room fill with drawings.
stops.quote: The lad was not only very expert with his mechanical tools, but he was equally so with his pen.
stops.quote_source: William Stukeley, memoir of Newton sent to Richard Mead in four instalments, 26 June to 22 July 1727 (Keynes Ms. 136.03, King's College Cambridge; Newton Project THEM00158). The 1752 Revised Memoir words the same recollection differently.
sources: King's School Grantham records, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: The carved windowsill at The King's School, Grantham, and Stukeley's 1727 memoir of the drawings on the lodging-room walls

stops.name: Woolsthorpe Manor, recalled to the sheep
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January
stops.campa: His mother, widowed a second time, takes him out of school to run the farm. He is sixteen and useless at it. He reads under hedgerows while the sheep walk into the neighbours' corn, and the manor court fines him for it. Within a year the schoolmaster Henry Stokes and his uncle the Reverend William Ayscough have talked Hannah round: the boy is being wasted on husbandry. Stokes offers to remit the fees and take him back into his own house. He goes back to Grantham to be prepared for Cambridge.
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: The Woolsthorpe manor court rolls recording fines for straying sheep

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, admitted subsizar
stops.date_confidence: attested, 5 June 1661, in the Trinity admissions register. This is the date of admission; he matriculated on 8 July. The research pool called the June date a matriculation.
stops.campa: He enters Trinity as a subsizar, the lowest rank the college keeps: he waits on wealthier undergraduates, fetches their meals, empties their basins, and pays his way with the work. His mother has an estate worth several hundred a year and does not fund him. He is nineteen, two or three years older than the men he serves at table, and he keeps his accounts and his grudges in the same notebook. Edward Bulwer-Lytton will matriculate into this same court a hundred and sixty years later, into a Trinity that by then trades on Newton's name.
sources: Trinity College admissions register, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: The Trinity College admissions register entry of 5 June 1661

stops.name: Trinity College, the list of sins
stops.date_confidence: the list is headed 'before Whitsunday 1662', which falls in May that year; the exact day of writing is unknown. The quotes lens of the pool placed this entry at Woolsthorpe; the Fitzwilliam Notebook is a Cambridge notebook.
stops.campa: Before his first communion he sets down, in a private shorthand, a list of forty-nine sins committed before Whitsunday. Most are small: eating an apple at church, making a mousetrap on the Lord's day, punching his sister, swimming in a tub on Sunday. One is not small. Between the mousetrap and the pie he records what he once wished on the household at North Witham. It sits in the list at the same weight as the apple and the tub, unmarked and unexplained. He is nineteen, and writing for no reader.
stops.quote: Threatening my father and mother Smith to burn them and the house over them.
stops.quote_source: Newton's list of sins committed before Whitsunday 1662, Fitzwilliam Notebook, Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: The Fitzwilliam Notebook and its shorthand list of sins, Whitsunday 1662

stops.name: Trinity College, the scholar and the motto
stops.date_confidence: the scholarship year 1664 is attested by MacTutor; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. The notebook motto was added above the title at an undetermined date in the same period.
stops.campa: He is elected a scholar of Trinity, which buys him four years of funding and the freedom to stop waiting at table. Isaac Barrow examines him; the college tradition that Barrow found him weak on Euclid and strong on Descartes comes from Conduitt half a century later and is not evidence. In a notebook he has been filling with headings of his own devising, the Quaestiones quaedam philosophicae, he writes a Latin tag above the title. It is a schoolman's commonplace, copied from the schools he is reading against, and it stands above pages of notes on Descartes, Boyle, and Hobbes.
stops.quote: Amicus Plato amicus Aristoteles magis amica veritas
stops.quote_source: Motto added above the title of the Quaestiones quaedam philosophicae, Cambridge University Library MS Add. 3996. Rendered: Plato is my friend, Aristotle is my friend, but a greater friend is truth. The English wording in circulation is a translator's, not Newton's.
sources: Conduitt memoranda, Keynes MS 130 (late and disputed)
suggested_refs: Cambridge University Library MS Add. 3996, the Quaestiones notebook

stops.name: Stourbridge Common, the prism at the fair
stops.date_confidence: contested three ways and not resolved here: the research pool gave 1663, Wikipedia's Stourbridge Fair article gives 1665, and Newton's own 1672 letter, the source of the quoted line, says 'the beginning of the Year 1666'. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: On the common outside Cambridge the greatest fair in England sets up its booths for a fortnight: cloth, horses, hops, iron, and the glass trinkets sold as toys. He buys a triangular prism there. It is a child's curiosity, priced as one, and he takes it back to his rooms, bores a hole in the shutter, and lets a single beam of sun fall through the glass onto the far wall. The band of colours it throws is about five times longer than it is broad, which no account of light taught in the schools allows. He measures it, and writes the measurement down.
stops.quote: I procured me a triangular glass-prism, to try therewith the celebrated phenomena of colours.
stops.quote_source: Newton's recollection, reported in David Brewster, Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton (Edinburgh, 1855)
suggested_refs: Stourbridge Common, Cambridge, site of the fair, and the surviving stub of the Leper Chapel

stops.name: Woolsthorpe Manor, the university shuts
stops.date_confidence: Cambridge closed in the summer of 1665 as the Great Plague reached the town; the month given here is conventional and the day is not attested
stops.campa: The plague comes up from London and the university sends everyone home. He rides back to Lincolnshire with his notebooks and stays, apart from one short return, until the spring of 1667. There is no library at Woolsthorpe and no one to talk to. There is a garden, a shuttered upper room, and a stack of paper. He is twenty-two, has taken an undistinguished degree, and has published nothing. In the eighteen months that follow he fills the paper, and shows almost none of it to anybody for twenty years.
suggested_refs: The upper chamber at Woolsthorpe Manor, with the shutter Newton bored for the prism experiment

stops.name: Woolsthorpe Manor, the prime of my age for invention
stops.date_confidence: the work is spread across 1665 and 1666 and cannot be dated to a day; 01 January stands for the whole of the annus mirabilis, which Newton himself dated only by the two plague years
stops.campa: In the shuttered room he works out the method of fluxions, which is the differential calculus; the inverse method, which is the integral; the binomial theorem in general form; the composition of white light out of the whole spectrum, proved by passing the divided beam through a second prism and finding it will divide no further; and the reach of the inverse-square law from a falling body out to the orbit of the moon. He tells nobody. He publishes none of it for decades, and half of it never. Fifty years later he sets down what those months were.
stops.quote: All this was in the two plague years of 1665 and 1666, for in those days I was in the prime of my age for invention, and minded Mathematicks and Philosophy more than at any time since.
stops.quote_source: Newton, undated autobiographical memorandum, c. 1716, Cambridge University Library MS Add. 3968
suggested_refs: Cambridge University Library MS Add. 3968, Newton's own account of the plague years

stops.name: Woolsthorpe Manor, the apple in the orchard
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The anecdote comes from Newton himself in old age, transmitted by Stukeley in 1752; historians dispute how literally to read it, and no month or day is attested. The date given is conventional.
stops.campa: He sits in the garden after dinner, under the apple trees, in the scene Stukeley writes down eighty-six years later from Newton's own telling of it. An apple falls. Why always perpendicularly to the ground, he asks, and why not sideways or upward, and if the power reaches to the top of the tree, why should it not reach further, to the moon, and hold her in her course as the apple is held to the earth. The tree is a Flower of Kent. It blew down in 1820 and grew again from its own roots, and the rings say it is over four hundred years old.
stops.quote: why should that apple always descend perpendicularly to the ground
stops.quote_source: William Stukeley, Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life (1752), reporting a conversation with Newton in his last years
suggested_refs: The Flower of Kent apple tree in the orchard at Woolsthorpe Manor, regrown from the roots of the tree felled in 1820

stops.name: Trinity College, minor fellow and major fellow
stops.date_confidence: attested, 2 October 1667, in the Trinity records; the geography lens of the pool gave 1 October. The major fellowship followed in July 1668 with the MA.
stops.campa: The university reopens and he comes back to a fellowship election he might easily have lost, since nine places are filled and he has spent two years absent with nothing published. He is chosen. Rooms, a stipend, and no obligation to teach anyone follow. The next July he takes his master's degree and the senior fellowship. He buys chemical glassware, two furnaces, and a copy of the Theatrum Chemicum, and sets up a laboratory in the strip of garden between his rooms and the chapel. He is twenty-five and no longer answerable to anybody.
sources: Trinity College records, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: Newton's rooms on the north side of Great Gate, Trinity College, and the garden laboratory beside them

stops.name: Trinity College, the mirror ground by hand
stops.date_confidence: the first instrument is dated 1668 by Wikipedia's article on Newton's reflector; the pool's geography lens dated the telescopes 1670 to 1672, which is late. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Having shown that a lens must split light into colours and blur every image it makes, he builds a telescope that uses no lens to gather with. He casts the alloy himself, grinds and polishes the concave mirror himself, mounts it in a tube six inches long, and gets a magnification of about forty. Nobody in England has made one work before. Barrow carries a second instrument down to London at the end of 1671; it is shown to Charles II in January and passed hand to hand around the Royal Society, and the Society elects the man who made it.
sources: Royal Society archives, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: Newton's second reflecting telescope, preserved in the Royal Society collections, London

stops.name: Trinity College, Barrow stands down from the Lucasian chair
stops.date_confidence: attested, 29 October 1669, in the Cambridge University records
stops.campa: Isaac Barrow resigns the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics in favour of his own student and goes to London to be a divine. Newton, twenty-six, takes a chair he will hold for thirty-two years, with a statutory duty of one lecture a week in term and no duty at all to be listened to. His first course, delivered in 1670, is on optics, and often he speaks to an empty room and goes back upstairs. Two and a half centuries later Paul Dirac holds the same chair, which by then is known chiefly as the one that was Newton's.
sources: Cambridge University records, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: The Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics, founded 1663, and its lecture deposit copies in Cambridge University Library

stops.name: Arundel House, the Strand: elected, and the light divided
stops.date_confidence: attested, 11 January 1672, Royal Society Journal Book. The venue is corrected: the Society sat at Arundel House from 1666 until 1673, not at Gresham College as the pool's geography lens had it. The optical paper was Newton's letter of 6 February, read on 8 February and printed on 19 February.
stops.campa: The Royal Society, meeting in the Duke of Norfolk's house on the Strand because the Great Fire took Gresham College, elects him a Fellow on the strength of the telescope. Four weeks later his first paper is read aloud to the room: white light is not simple and pure but a heterogeneous mixture of rays of every colour, and the prism does not manufacture the colours, it only separates what was there. Robert Hooke answers the same week that the whole thing is wrong. A century and a half on, Goethe will write a book against it and prize that book above his poems.
suggested_refs: Arundel House on the Strand, seat of the Royal Society 1666-1673, demolished 1678

stops.name: Trinity College, the laboratory beside the rooms
stops.date_confidence: the annotation quoted is dated 1675; the alchemical work itself runs without interruption from about 1669 into the 1690s and cannot be dated to a day. Month and day default to 01 January.
stops.campa: Behind the wall of his rooms the furnaces run for weeks at a time, sometimes through the night, and his assistant reports that the fires go out neither in spring nor at harvest. He is not doing chemistry as the Society understands it. He is reading Sendivogius and Philalethes, transcribing recipes for the green lion and the star regulus of antimony, and building a corpus of more than a million words that he will never publish and will partly burn. Ezechiel Foxcroft hands him an anonymous tract called Manna, and he writes across it what he takes the work to be.
stops.quote: This philosophy, both speculative and active, is not only to be found in the volume of nature, but also in the sacred scriptures.
stops.quote_source: Newton's 1675 annotation to the anonymous alchemical tract 'Manna, a disquisition of the nature of alchemy'. Reported in secondary literature only: Laurence Gardner, The Shadow of Solomon (2007), p. 146, via Wikipedia. No manuscript transcription was reached; the Newton Project corpus search returned nothing for this wording.
sources: Chymistry of Isaac Newton project, Indiana University
Gardner, The Shadow of Solomon (2007), p. 146, at one remove
suggested_refs: The Newton alchemical manuscripts digitised by the Chymistry of Isaac Newton project, Indiana University

stops.name: Trinity College Chapel, the dispensation from holy orders
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1675 by the royal warrant; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: The statutes require every fellow to take holy orders within seven years or vacate his place, and his seven years are running out. He cannot swear to the Trinity. He has been reading the Church Fathers for a decade and has concluded that Athanasius corrupted the scriptures, that the doctrine of the coeternal Son is a fourth-century forgery, and that the college named for that doctrine is built on a lie. He does not say so aloud; the penalty is ruin. Charles II grants the Lucasian Professor a dispensation in perpetuity, and the question is never asked again.
stops.quote: Atheism is so senseless and odious to mankind that it never had many professors.
stops.quote_source: Newton, A Short Scheme of the True Religion, manuscript, Keynes MS 7, King's College, Cambridge
sources: Royal warrant of April 1675, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: The Yahuda theological manuscripts, in which Newton's anti-Trinitarian argument is set out at length

stops.name: Trinity College, the letter to Hooke
stops.date_confidence: attested, 5 February 1675/6, in Turnbull's edition of the Correspondence. Seen at one remove through Wikipedia's citation of Turnbull; the printed volume was not opened.
stops.campa: Four years of quarrelling with Hooke over who first understood light have made him threaten to abandon philosophy altogether. A truce is patched up by letter, and in the middle of a courteous paragraph he writes the sentence that is now milled around the rim of the British two-pound coin. Read straight it is modesty. Read against the fact that Hooke is short and crooked-backed, it is something else, and both readings have been in print for three hundred years. Three years later the two men correspond about orbits and inverse squares, and the quarrel restarts and never stops.
stops.quote: If I have seen further it is by standing on ye sholders of Giants.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Robert Hooke, 5 February 1675/6, in The Correspondence of Isaac Newton, ed. H. W. Turnbull, Vol. I (Cambridge, 1959), p. 416. Newton's spelling.
sources: Turnbull, ed., Correspondence of Isaac Newton, Vol. I, p. 416, via Wikipedia
suggested_refs: The Newton-Hooke correspondence of 1675-1680, printed in Turnbull's edition

stops.name: Trinity College, Halley's question
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1684 by De Moivre's account, recorded by Conduitt; the day is not given
stops.campa: Edmond Halley rides up from London with a question that he, Hooke, and Wren have failed to answer between them: what curve would a planet describe if it were drawn to the sun by a force falling off as the square of the distance. An ellipse, says Newton, without pausing. Halley asks how he knows. I have calculated it, he says, and goes to look for the paper, and cannot find it. He promises to work it again. What he sends down instead, over the next eighteen months of forgotten meals and unslept nights, is a new physics.
sources: Abraham De Moivre's account, recorded by Conduitt, Keynes MS 130
Humphrey Newton's recollections, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
suggested_refs: De Moivre's memorandum of the 1684 visit, Keynes MS 130, King's College Cambridge

stops.name: Gresham College, Book I laid before the Society
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 April 1686, in the Royal Society Council minutes. The Society had returned to Gresham College by this date; the pool gave a loose Bishopsgate pin.
stops.campa: The manuscript of the first book, De motu corporum, is presented to the Society, which votes at once that it be printed and then discovers it has spent its printing budget on a history of fishes. Halley undertakes the whole cost out of his own pocket, on a clerk's salary, and spends the next fifteen months editing the text, correcting the proofs, and talking Newton out of suppressing Book III in a rage when Hooke claims the inverse-square law as his own. Halley never claims a share of the work. His name appears in the book once, on a Latin ode printed at the front.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's registered copy of De motu corporum in gyrum, 1684

stops.name: London, Streater's press
stops.date_confidence: July 1687 is attested; the day is not. The '5 July' in circulation appears to come from confusion with the licensing a year earlier, when the Society ordered the book printed on 30 June 1686 and Pepys signed the imprimatur in July 1686.
stops.campa: Joseph Streater prints Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica for the Royal Society, five hundred copies or so, licensed by Samuel Pepys as president. Three laws of motion and one law of gravitation carry the tides, the precession of the equinoxes, the flattening of the earth at the poles, and the path of the comet of 1680. The system holds without correction for two hundred and thirty-two years, until an eclipse photographed off the coast of Africa gives Einstein twice Newton's figure for the bending of starlight.
suggested_refs: Newton's own annotated copy of the first edition, Cambridge University Library, Adv.b.39.1

stops.name: Palace of Westminster, the member for Cambridge University
stops.date_confidence: the Convention Parliament assembled 22 January 1689; Newton's own first attendance is not separately dated in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Two years earlier he had stood with the fellows who refused James II's order to grant a Benedictine monk a degree without the oaths, and had gone to London with the deputation that faced down Judge Jeffreys. The university remembers, and returns him to the Convention Parliament that settles the crown on William and Mary. He sits thirteen months. The tradition that he rose only once, to ask that a window be shut, is told by his biographers and doubted by them in the same breath. No parliamentary record confirms it.
sources: Cambridge University Grace Book, cited in Westfall
Brewster, Memoirs of Newton (anecdote, disputed as apocryphal)
suggested_refs: The Cambridge University deputation of 1687 before the Ecclesiastical Commission

stops.name: Trinity College, the letter to Bentley
stops.date_confidence: attested, 25 February 1692/3, second of the four letters to Richard Bentley
stops.campa: Richard Bentley, preparing the first Boyle Lectures, writes to ask whether the Principia proves a God. Newton answers in four letters that the system of the world could not have arranged itself, and then, pressed on what gravity actually is, refuses the one thing every reader wants from him. He will not say that matter attracts matter across empty space by its own nature. Something must mediate, material or not, and he does not know what. A century later Mesmer will take Newtonian action at a distance, and Newton's own speculative aether with it, and pour both into the human body.
stops.quote: Tis inconceivable that inanimate brute matter should (without the mediation of something else which is not material) operate upon & affect other matter without mutual contact.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Richard Bentley, 25 February 1692/3, in Four Letters from Sir Isaac Newton to Doctor Bentley
suggested_refs: Four Letters from Sir Isaac Newton to Doctor Bentley, published 1756

stops.name: Trinity College, the September letters
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1693 by the letters themselves; the accusatory letter to Pepys is dated 13 September and that to Locke 16 September
stops.campa: He writes to Samuel Pepys that he must withdraw from his acquaintance and see neither him nor any of his friends again. He writes to John Locke that he had thought Locke was trying to embroil him with women, and that he had wished him dead, and asks pardon. He tells both men he has not slept an hour a night for a fortnight. Within weeks he is himself again and apologising for a distemper he blames on bad sleep and worse diet. What caused it is argued still: overwork, a fire among his papers, the mercury.
sources: Newton's letters to Pepys and Locke, September 1693, in the Correspondence
suggested_refs: The September 1693 letters to Pepys and Locke, printed in Turnbull's edition of the Correspondence

stops.name: Royal Mint, Tower of London: the Warden
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1696 by the Treasury warrant; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Charles Montagu gets him the wardenship of the Mint, understood on all sides as a comfortable sinecure for a great man gone stale. He takes lodgings inside the Tower, where the presses run twenty hours a day recoining the whole silver currency of England, and discovers that the office carries a criminal jurisdiction no previous warden has troubled to use. He takes depositions in alehouses, runs informers in the Fleet and the King's Bench, cross-examines suspects himself, and prosecutes twenty-eight coiners to conviction.
sources: Treasury warrant, April 1696, cited in Westfall, Never at Rest
Thomas Levenson, Newton and the Counterfeiter (2009)
suggested_refs: The Mint records of Newton's depositions, National Archives, Kew

stops.name: Newgate and Tyburn, the end of William Chaloner
stops.date_confidence: trial at the Old Bailey attested to 3 March 1699; the hanging at Tyburn followed on 22 March. The pool's entry placed the execution at Newgate, which is wrong: Chaloner was held there, not hanged there.
stops.campa: William Chaloner has counterfeited the new milled coinage, forged Bank of England notes, and petitioned Parliament that the Mint itself be investigated for incompetence, naming its Warden. Newton takes two years to bury him. He collects statements from Chaloner's associates, wives, and gaolers, keeps him in Newgate while the evidence is assembled, and puts the case to the Old Bailey in March. Chaloner writes from the condemned cell begging the Warden for his life and calling him merciful. He is drawn to Tyburn and hanged on the twenty-second.
sources: Old Bailey Proceedings and Newgate records, 1699
suggested_refs: Chaloner's letters to Newton from the condemned hold at Newgate, Mint papers, National Archives

stops.name: Royal Mint, Tower of London: Master of the Mint
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1699 by the Treasury warrant; the day is not given
stops.campa: The mastership falls vacant and he takes it, with a salary and a percentage on every pound coined that will make him a rich man. He holds it twenty-eight years, to the end of his life, and audits it as though the coin were his own. In 1717, asked by the Treasury to fix the value of the gold guinea against silver, he sets it at twenty-one shillings, undervaluing silver enough that it flows out of the country and gold stays. He does not intend to put England on a gold standard. England is on one for two hundred years.
suggested_refs: Newton's 1717 report to the Treasury on the value of gold and silver coin

stops.name: Trinity College, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Trinity records; the month is not given in the reachable sources and defaults to 01 January
stops.campa: He resigns the Lucasian Professorship and the Trinity fellowship together, thirty-five years after walking in as a servant to richer boys. He has not lived in Cambridge for five years and has not lectured for longer. Whiston takes the chair as his deputy and then in his own right. The rooms are cleared, the furnaces cold, the garden laboratory dismantled. He keeps the manuscripts. Everything he wrote in this college that he judged fit to print is already printed, and it comes to two books.
suggested_refs: William Whiston's account of succeeding Newton in the Lucasian chair

stops.name: Gresham College, President of the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested, 30 November 1703, St Andrew's Day, the Society's anniversary meeting. The venue is corrected: the Society did not acquire Crane Court until 26 October 1710 and in 1703 still met at Gresham College.
stops.campa: Hooke dies in March and Newton stands for the presidency in November, on the anniversary day, and is elected. He is sixty-one. He holds the chair by annual re-election for twenty-four years and runs the Society as a Mint: attendance registers, an experiment at every meeting, committees appointed and reporting, a purpose-built house bought in Crane Court in 1710. Fellows who cross him find themselves off the Council. Hooke's portrait, if the Society owned one, does not survive the move.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Journal Books of Newton's presidency, 1703-1727

stops.name: Jermyn Street, the Opticks in English
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The house is corrected: the pool placed the Opticks at St Martin's Street, where Newton did not live until 1710. In 1704 he was on Jermyn Street.
stops.campa: He waits until Hooke is dead and then publishes the optical work of forty years, in English, in a plain style, with the experiments given so that any reader can repeat them. At the end he appends the Queries, thirty-one open questions in which he says what he will not assert: on the nature of light, the forces between the smallest parts of bodies, and whether the system of the world needs occasional divine repair. He keeps house here with his niece Catherine Barton, whose wit is famous across London.
stops.quote: For while Comets move in very excentrick Orbs in all manner of Positions, blind Fate could never make all the Planets move one and the same way in Orbs concentrick, some inconsiderable Irregularities excepted, which may have risen from the mutual Actions of Comets and Planets upon one another, and which will be apt to increase, till this System wants a Reformation.
stops.quote_source: Opticks, Query 31, 4th edition (London, William Innys, 1730), text verified against Project Gutenberg ebook 33504
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: The Queries appended to the Opticks, expanded through the editions of 1706, 1717, and 1730

stops.name: Trinity College, Queen Anne's sword
stops.date_confidence: attested, 16 April 1705, in the Cambridge University records. Popular accounts that place the ceremony at Whitehall are wrong; the queen was in Cambridge.
stops.campa: Anne comes to Cambridge in April and knights him in the college where he waited at table forty-four years before. He is the second man of science ever knighted in England and the first for anything resembling philosophy, though the honour is generally read as payment for a Whig candidacy in the university election a month later. He loses the election. He keeps the title. From here he is Sir Isaac, and that is the form of the name every English schoolroom keeps afterwards.
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: Queen Anne's progress to Cambridge, April 1705, and the Trinity Master's Lodge ceremony

stops.name: St Martin's Street, the house at Leicester Fields
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. He lived here until 1725.
stops.campa: He moves to a narrow brick house on St Martin's Street off Leicester Fields, with an observatory built out on the roof and a household run by Catherine Barton and, after her marriage, by her husband John Conduitt. Visitors come to look at him. He is the most famous living Englishman, keeps six red-upholstered rooms, sits for a dozen portraits, and gives away money quietly to relatives he has barely met. The house stands until the twentieth century and is pulled down still known to the neighbourhood as Newton's House.
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: Newton's House, St Martin's Street, Leicester Fields, photographed before demolition

stops.name: Crane Court, the committee on the calculus
stops.date_confidence: the committee was appointed and reported in 1712 and the Commercium Epistolicum was printed the same year; month and day default to 01 January
stops.campa: Leibniz, who published the differential calculus in 1684 while Newton's fluxions sat unprinted in a drawer, appeals to the Royal Society to settle who was first. The Society appoints a committee. The committee is chosen by the president, sits in the president's building, and delivers a verdict for the president; the Commercium Epistolicum that prints its findings is largely drafted by Newton himself, and so is the anonymous review of it that appears in the Philosophical Transactions. Both men had it independently. Only one of them controlled the court.
suggested_refs: Commercium Epistolicum D. Johannis Collins et aliorum de analysi promota, London, 1712

stops.name: Cambridge, the second edition and the General Scholium
stops.date_confidence: attested, 30 June 1713, 750 copies. The place is corrected: the 1713 imprint reads Cantabrigiae, Cambridge. The pool's geography lens said London and contradicted its own chronology lens.
stops.campa: Roger Cotes edits the second edition at Cambridge under Bentley's eye, arguing Newton into corrections through two hundred letters and dying three years later at thirty-three. Newton adds a closing General Scholium: the elegant system of sun and planets could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being, and as for what gravity itself is, he declines to invent. The Latin runs to three words. Motte's English of 1729 is set down here as Motte wrote it.
stops.quote: But hitherto I have not been able to discover the cause of those properties of gravity from phenomena, and I frame no hypotheses; for whatever is not deduced from the phenomena is to be called an hypothesis; and hypotheses, whether metaphysical or physical, whether of occult qualities or mechanical, have no place in experimental philosophy.
stops.quote_source: Principia, Book III, General Scholium, added in the second edition of 1713, trans. Andrew Motte (1729), verified against the Internet Archive text newtonspmathema00newtrich. Latin: hypotheses non fingo.
sources: Motte's English Principia, 1729, Internet Archive newtonspmathema00newtrich
suggested_refs: The Newton-Cotes correspondence on the second edition, 1709-1713

stops.name: St Martin's Street, the kingdoms remeasured
stops.date_confidence: no single date. The chronological and prophetic manuscripts run from the 1680s to his death and were printed posthumously in 1728; 1720 stands for the late London phase of the work.
stops.campa: Upstairs, unpublished, runs the other half of the life: a chronology of the ancient world rebuilt from eclipse records and the precession of the equinoxes, which shortens Greek history by three centuries and redates the reign of Nebuchadnezzar; a reconstruction of the Temple of Solomon from the cubits given in Ezekiel, treated as the key to the whole scheme; and a reading of Daniel and the Apocalypse. He calculates a date past which the prophecy cannot run, and says plainly why he calculates it.
stops.quote: This I mention not to assert when the time of the end shall be, but to put a stop to the rash conjectures of fancifull men who are frequently predicting the time of the end, & by doing so bring the sacred prophesies into discredit as often as their predictions fail.
stops.quote_source: Yahuda MS 7.3g, f. 13v, National Library of Israel, from the passage that arrives at the year 2060
sources: Yahuda MS 7.3g, National Library of Israel
suggested_refs: The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended, published posthumously, London, 1728

stops.name: Kensington, the boy on the sea-shore
stops.date_confidence: the move to Kensington is dated 1725 and the remark is undated. Brewster reports it in 1855 as something Newton said shortly before his death; it is a secondhand attribution, not a manuscript in Newton's hand.
stops.campa: In failing health he takes a house at Kensington for the air, and the Conduitts move him out of the London smoke. He is eighty-two. He gives up going in to the Mint except on the great occasions, sits for more portraits, corrects the third edition of the Principia for Henry Pemberton, and receives visitors who write down everything he says. To one of them he gives an account of his own work. Brewster prints it a hundred and thirty years later and names no witness for it.
stops.quote: I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.
stops.quote_source: Reported by David Brewster, Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton (Edinburgh, 1855), Vol. II, Ch. 27
sources: Brewster, Memoirs of Newton (1855), Vol. II, Ch. 27
Conduitt's account of Newton's last years, Keynes MS 130
suggested_refs: Conduitt's memoranda of Newton's conversation in the Kensington years, Keynes MS 130

stops.name: Kensington, death in his sleep
stops.date_confidence: 20 March 1727 Old Style, 31 March 1727 New Style. Sources lead with one or the other and disagree; both are given here rather than choosing.
stops.campa: He goes into London on the last day of February to preside at the Royal Society, comes back exhausted, and takes to his bed with the stone. The pain is such that the sweat runs off his face, and he laughs and talks between the fits. On the Saturday evening he loses consciousness and does not recover it, and he dies in the small hours of Monday, eighty-four years old. He refuses the sacrament of the Church of England on his deathbed. Those attending record it and do not print it, and the meaning of the refusal is left where he left it.
sources: Westfall, Never at Rest, cited through the research pool
suggested_refs: Conduitt's narrative of Newton's last illness, Keynes MS 130, King's College Cambridge

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the state funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 March 1727, Westminster Abbey burial register and the Abbey's own commemorations record
stops.campa: He lies in state in the Jerusalem Chamber and is carried into the nave by the Lord Chancellor, the Dukes of Montrose and Roxburgh, and the Earls of Pembroke, Sussex, and Macclesfield. The grave is cut before the choir screen, in ground until now given to kings, princes, and abbots. Voltaire is in the crowd, exiled and watching, and writes afterwards that England buries its mathematicians as it buries its monarchs. The dead man held no office in church or state except the Mint.
sources: Westminster Abbey, official commemorations page for Sir Isaac Newton
Voltaire, Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733)
suggested_refs: Newton's grave slab in the nave of Westminster Abbey, before the choir screen

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the monument and the refused couplet
stops.date_confidence: the Abbey's own record states the monument was finished in August 1730 and unveiled the following year. The pool's geography lens gave only 1731; both dates are correct for different acts.
stops.campa: Michael Rysbrack carves the monument to William Kent's design: a reclining Newton in white and grey marble, leaning on four books lettered Divinity, Chronology, Opticks, and Philo. Prin. Math., with boys below handling a prism, a telescope, and the coining apparatus of the Mint, and above him a globe on which the comet of 1680 traces its path. The Latin inscription tells mortals to rejoice that so great an ornament of the human race has existed. Alexander Pope writes a couplet for it. The Abbey refuses the couplet.
stops.quote: Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night: God said, Let Newton be! and all was light
stops.quote_source: Alexander Pope's proposed epitaph for the Newton monument, declined by Westminster Abbey
sources: Westminster Abbey, official commemorations page for Sir Isaac Newton
suggested_refs: The Rysbrack and Kent monument against the choir screen, Westminster Abbey

stops.name: Paris, the Marquise translates the Principia
stops.date_confidence: Emilie du Chatelet completed the translation in 1749, the year she died; first publication 1756, second edition 1759. The pool's afterlife lens gave 1759 for the translation itself, which is the later edition. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Emilie du Chatelet renders the whole of the Principia into French and adds a commentary that recasts Newton's geometry in the calculus of the continent, finishing the manuscript in the last months of a pregnancy she does not survive. It appears seven years after her death and has never been superseded: it is still the only complete French Principia. Through her the book crosses into a Europe that reads it in Latin at Konigsberg, where Martin Knutzen puts Newton into Kant's hands, and at Brunswick, where the boy Gauss finds him on a shelf.
suggested_refs: Principes mathematiques de la philosophie naturelle, trans. la Marquise du Chastellet, Paris, 1756

stops.name: Tate Britain, Newton on the seafloor
stops.date_confidence: the monotype is dated 1795 and was reworked and reprinted around 1805; month and day unknown. The pin is the work's present home, not the place of making, which was Lambeth.
stops.campa: William Blake prints a colour monotype of a naked young man crouched on a rock at the bottom of the sea, bent over a scroll, drawing a triangle with a pair of compasses and seeing nothing but the triangle. He calls it Newton. It is not an honour. In 1802, writing from Felpham, Blake names Newton with Locke as the single vision and Newton's sleep that his own fourfold seeing is set against. In 1995 Eduardo Paolozzi casts the same figure twelve feet high in bronze and sets it in the piazza of the British Library.
suggested_refs: Blake's Newton, colour print finished in ink and watercolour, Tate Britain; Paolozzi's bronze, British Library piazza

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the nave fills
stops.date_confidence: Kelvin's burial attested to 23 December 1907; the Dirac memorial stone was unveiled 13 November 1995. One pin, two dates, and this stop carries the earlier.
stops.campa: Lord Kelvin is buried in the nave immediately south of the grave, and the Abbey records the placement as being beside Newton. In 1995 a floor-stone for Paul Dirac is set near the same slab, cut with his equation, for a man who had held the Lucasian chair from 1932. Herschel, Darwin, Rutherford, and Hawking all come in afterwards, and all come in within a few yards of the same paving. The scientists' corner of the Abbey takes its shape from one slab cut in 1727.
suggested_refs: The scientists' corner of the Westminster Abbey nave, grouped around Newton's grave

stops.name: Sotheby's, New Bond Street: the Portsmouth Papers
stops.date_confidence: the sale year 1936 is attested; the month and day are not given in the reachable sources and default to 01 January
stops.campa: The Earl of Portsmouth's family sends to auction the papers Cambridge would not take: some three hundred and twenty-nine lots, more than a third of them alchemical, judged at Newton's death not fit to be printed and left in a box for two centuries. John Maynard Keynes buys most of the alchemy, and the death mask with it, and spends ten years reading what he has bought. In 1946 he tells the Royal Society Club what he found, and it is not the founder of the age of reason.
stops.quote: Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians, the last of the Babylonians and Sumerians.
stops.quote_source: John Maynard Keynes, 'Newton, the Man', written for the 1942 tercentenary and read to the Royal Society Club in 1946
suggested_refs: The Sotheby's sale catalogue of the Newton papers, 1936; the Keynes Newton collection, King's College Cambridge

stops.name: Jerusalem, the theological papers
stops.date_confidence: the Yahuda collection reached the National Library of Israel in 1969 after litigation; month and day unknown. The pool reproduced a Wikipedia error making the Keynes papers pass to Yahuda: they did not. Keynes bequeathed his collection to King's College, Cambridge in 1946.
stops.campa: Abraham Yahuda buys the theological manuscripts at the same 1936 sale, the ones on Daniel, the Apocalypse, the corruption of scripture by Athanasius, and the measurement of Solomon's Temple. They go to Jerusalem, to the National Library of Israel, and sit largely unread for a further thirty years. Then the Newton Project and the Chymistry project photograph everything and put it online, and the private half of the life becomes public in full: four million words that the state funeral was not held for.
sources: National Library of Israel, Yahuda Papers
suggested_refs: The Yahuda Newton manuscripts, National Library of Israel, Jerusalem, digitised by the Newton Project
